title: Thermodynamic description of wealth inequality in the world
authors: Klaus M. Frahm, Leonardo Ermann, Dima L. Shepelyansky
abstract: According to the recent Wealth Thermalization Hypothesis (WTH) the wealth inequality in the world is described by the Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) thermal distribution of interacting agents in a society with social stratification. In this concept, the wealth layers of society are associated with energy levels from a nonlinear dynamical system conserving two integrals of motion being total energy and probability norm. This leads to RJ condensation and the formation of a huge poverty phase of low wealth and a tiny oligarchic phase that captures a main part of total society wealth. This RJ phenomenon has similarities with self cleaning in multimode optical fibers and constraint driven condensation in various physical systems. We analyze real Lorenz and Pareto curves for wealth of households in countries and the world, Gross Domestic Product of countries, market capitalization of companies at stock exchange of Hong Kong, Shanghai, London, bitcoin transactions, world trade between countries and show that the WTH theory gives a good description of these curves. On the basis of this comparison we argue that the RJ thermal distribution provides a universal description of wealth inequality in the world.
summary: This paper applies statistical mechanics principles, specifically the Wealth Thermalization Hypothesis (WTH), to model global wealth inequality. It shows that the Rayleigh-Jeans thermal distribution accurately describes empirical data for household wealth and national GDP across decades. The work argues that this thermodynamic condensation mechanism provides a universal physical law governing social stratification.
main_problem: To provide a thermodynamic description of global wealth inequality using the Wealth Thermalization Hypothesis (WTH).
main_result: The Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) thermal distribution provides a universal and good description for various real-world curves related to wealth inequality, such as Lorenz curves for household wealth, GDP, and stock markets.
method: The analysis involves deriving analytical expressions for the Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient using continuous models like RJS and RJE spectra, and fitting these theoretical predictions to empirical economic data.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as 'Social Stratification in a Society' (SSS) where wealth layers are associated with energy levels governed by a nonlinear dynamical system conserving total energy and probability norm. The core model uses the RJS and RJE spectra derived from statistical mechanics principles.
key_observables: Lorenz curve ($w$ vs $h$), Gini Coefficient ($G$), Pareto Probability Distribution ($C(w_m)$), Temperature ($T$), Chemical Potential ($\mu$).
important_parameters: The energy parameter $\epsilon$, the spectral parameters $a$, and the regime of condensation (e.g., low $\epsilon$ for strong inequality).
main_assumptions: The system undergoes dynamical thermalization governed by weak nonlinear perturbations, allowing the use of a grand canonical ensemble description.
figures_summary: Figures compare theoretical Lorenz curves (RJS/RJE) and Pareto distributions against real-world data for household wealth (World 2021), GDP evolution (UN data 1973–2023), and stock markets, demonstrating quantitative agreement.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the WTH framework to deriving analytical solutions for key diagnostics using RJS/RJE models. It then systematically applies these models by fitting parameters to diverse datasets (household wealth, GDP, etc.) to argue for universality.
why_interesting: It provides a powerful analogy between condensed matter physics concepts like thermalization and condensation (RJ phenomenon) and macroscopic socio-economic phenomena like global wealth distribution, suggesting universal physical laws govern social structures.
